I'll summarize below.\\n\\nMaya: Action list:\\n- A1: Add triage checklist for runtime OOMs (owner: Zia) \\u2014 include kubectl/logs, kv-cache check, fallback model switch. due 2026-05-03\\n- A2: Detection rule: recurring tokenization spike alert (owner: Ryan) \\u2014 alert when p50>200ms AND error_rate>0.5% for 5m. due 2026-05-06\\n- A3: Rollback/playbook for hot model rollout (owner: Sam) \\u2014 add escalation and automatic fallback. due 2026-05-10\\n\\nRyan: I'll take the detection rule. Proposed alert query:\\n```\\nsum by(model) (rate(redwood_inference_request_latency_seconds_bucket{le=\\\"0.2\\\"}[5m])) / sum by(model)(rate(redwood_inference_requests_total[5m])) < 0.8\\n```\\nWill add doc with thresholds and runbooks for false-positive tuning.\\n\\nZia: I'll update triage steps. Draft commands to include:\\n- kubectl -n inference logs -l app=redwood-runtime --tail=200\\n- kubectl exec -n inference svc/runtime -- /bin/sh -c \\\"cat /mnt/kvcache/stats || true\\\"\\n- curl -s https://api.redwood-internal/metrics?model=NAME | jq .latency\\nI'll open a PR to docs/runbooks/oom-troubleshoot.md and link here.\\n\\nSam: I'll own the rollback/playbook. {
  "channel": "incidents",
  "thread_ts": "1770004321",
  "first_message_ts": "1770004321",
  "last_message_ts": "1770004680",
  "participants": [
    "Maya",
    "Ryan",
    "Zia",
    "Sam",
    "ops-bot"
  ],
  "messages": "Maya: quick follow-up from the SEV-124 postmortem — we need runbook/playbook updates + owners for remediation items. I'll summarize below.

Maya: Action list:
- A1: Add triage checklist for runtime OOMs (owner: Zia) — include kubectl/logs, kv-cache check, fallback model switch. due 2026-05-03
- A2: Detection rule: recurring tokenization spike alert (owner: Ryan) — alert when p50>200ms AND error_rate>0.5% for 5m. due 2026-05-06
- A3: Rollback/playbook for hot model rollout (owner: Sam) — add escalation and automatic fallback. due 2026-05-10

Ryan: I'll take the detection rule. Proposed alert query:
```
sum by(model) (rate(redwood_inference_request_latency_seconds_bucket{le="0.2"}[5m])) / sum by(model)(rate(redwood_inference_requests_total[5m])) < 0.8
```
Will add doc with thresholds and runbooks for false-positive tuning.

Zia: I'll update triage steps. Draft commands to include:
- kubectl -n inference logs -l app=redwood-runtime --tail=200
- kubectl exec -n inference svc/runtime -- /bin/sh -c "cat /mnt/kvcache/stats || true"
- curl -s https://api.redwood-internal/metrics?model=NAME | jq .latency
I'll open a PR to docs/runbooks/oom-troubleshoot.md and link here.

Sam: I'll own the rollback/playbook. Escalation path proposal:
- 0-5m: Oncall (page, 2 min escalate)
- 5-15m: Eng-SRE (pager)
- 15-60m: Infra lead + Eng oncall + Customer Success (email)
Include fallback: switch to quantized variant or degrade to cached responses. I'll put steps and commands.

ops-bot: Reminder: created task TRACK-453 in action-tracker (https://go.track/453). assigned to Maya, due 2026-05-10.

Maya: For recurring pattern — let's add a periodic audit: weekly telemetry check for top-10 models and SLO drift. Ryan to add alert, Zia to add playbook step to run audit.

Ryan: noted. I'll create the alert + grafana dashboard panel (panel id TBD) and add runbook link.

Zia: PR link: https://github.com/redwood/runbooks/pull/312 — triage checklist added, still needs commands sanitized. target merge EOD 2026-04-28.

Sam: I'll draft the rollback playbook in docs/playbooks/hot-rollout-revert.md and ping @maya for review.

Maya: thanks all. Could folks add their owner tag in the action-tracker and set the due date? I'll follow up in weekly incident follow-up meeting.

Ryan: done :thumbsup:

Zia: added owner + due :white_check_mark:

Sam: added draft and owner. starting testing tomorrow.

Maya: closing thread once PRs merged and TRACK-453 is current. ping me on slack if blockers.",

  "content_field_names": [
    "messages"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_b7db94f4f13349948ae5d8303247897f"
}

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_63dc81476f6047fdbdf584c3bcd64f77",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-9402-canary-rollback-postmortem-actions-and-safety-automation.json",
    "title": "Canary rollout postmortem: automated safety gates, probe hysteresis, and rollback TTLs",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/linear",
    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"ENG-9402\",\n  \"team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"title\": \"Canary rollout postmortem: automated safety gates, probe hysteresis, and rollback TTLs\",\n  \"status\": \"In Progress\",\n  \"priority\": \"P0\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-02-20\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2025-03-05\",\n  \"creator\": \"Aisha Patel\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Marcelo Ruiz\",\n  \"project\": \"Model-lifecycle-tooling\",\n  \"cycle\": \"2025-W08\",\n  \"estimate\": \"5\",\n  \"due_date\": \"2025-03-12\",\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"canary-rollout\",\n    \"postmortem\",\n    \"auto-rollback\",\n    \"observability\",\n    \"runbook\"\n  ],\n  \"parent_issue\": [\n    \"ENG-8739\"\n  ],\n  \"dependencies\": [\n    \"ENG-7124\",\n    \"ENG-9021\"\n  ],\n  \"customer_impact\": \"high\",\n  \"release\": \"runtime-1.19\",\n  \"security_review_required\": \"false\",\n  \"description\": \"Summary: During a recent canary rollout of model v2.3 we observed a progressive increase in bad response rates across a small percentage of traffic and an eventual failed auto-rollback because the safety gate hysteresis allowed transient noise to be treated as stable regressions. This ticket captures the postmortem actions and tracks engineering work to harden canary safety gates, add automated sanity-runbooks, and implement a configurable rollback TTL and probe smoothing to avoid flapping.\\n\\nGoals: \\n- Collect incident learnings and formalize them into a canary safety runbook.\\n- Implement probe hysteresis and exponential backoff to reduce false positives from transient spikes.\\n- Add a rollback TTL and a circuit-breaker to prevent repeated rollbacks within short windows.\\n- Create automated canary dashboards and alert thresholds tied to traffic-weighted metrics.\\n- Add an audit log and post-deploy checklist that must pass before canary promotes beyond 5% traffic.\\n\\nScope: runtime canary controller, Redwood Console rollout UI, alerting rules in PagerDuty/Dashboards, runbook docs, and a follow-up QA pass on dedicated capacity behavior.\\n\\nSuccess criteria: \\n- New runbook published to Confluence with a clear escalation path and playbook steps.\\n- Canary controller implements smoothing and rollback TTL (configurable per-release).\\n- Observability dashboards with synthetic probe traces and traffic-weighted SLOs available in staging and production.\\n- One simulated canary test with injected faults runs cleanly (no false rollback) before rollout to customers.\\n\\nNotes: This is time-sensitive because the customer who triggered the incident is on a dedicated capacity contract and expects a write-up plus mitigations within 2 weeks.\",\n  \"comments\": [\n    \"2025-02-20 \\u2014 Aisha Patel: Filed after incident INC-2025-112. Initial triage: regression signature was 0.8% bad_response_rate at 3% traffic increasing to 2.6% over 30 minutes. Canary controller rolled back once then failed to re-promote; logs show hysteresis window configured at 5 minutes which allowed noisy spike to be interpreted as sustained regression.\",\n    \"2025-02-21 \\u2014 Marcelo Ruiz: Reproduced locally with traffic replay. Root cause appears to be twofold: (1) probe smoothing configured as simple moving average with short window; (2) rollback policy lacks TTL so subsequent canary promotions immediately retriggered the same checks. Drafting patch for smoothing and TTL config in canary controller.\",\n    \"2025-02-24 \\u2014 SRE Review (Lindsey Wong): Recommended adding median-based probe plus percentile trimming to avoid outlier-driven signals. Also suggested a temporary alert to page on 1.5% sustained bad_response_rate over 20 minutes during canary windows.\",\n    \"2025-02-27 \\u2014 Design (Hiro Tanaka): Console UX update: expose a 'safety profile' selector (conservative, balanced, aggressive) with defaults and per-release overrides. Planned mockups linked.\",\n    \"2025-03-02 \\u2014 Marcelo Ruiz: Draft PR submitted implementing exponential smoothing (alpha configurable) and rollback_ttl_seconds with default 3600s. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4821\",\n    \"2025-03-04 \\u2014 QA (Priya Desai): Ran canary simulation with injected 0.5% latency noise and 2x error spikes for 3 minutes \\u2014 no false positive rollback after smoothing enabled; TTL prevented immediate re-rollouts. Pending integration tests in dedicated capacity environment.\"\n  ],\n  \"attachments\": [\n    \"Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/Canary+Safety+Runbook\",\n    \"Incident: INC-2025-112 (internal) https://redwood.incidents/INC-2025-112\",\n    \"GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4821\",\n    \"Dashboard (staging): https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/rollouts/canary-health?orgId=1\"\n  ],\n  \"decision_log\": [\n    \"2025-02-22: Agreed to implement exponential smoothing (configurable alpha) rather than longer simple moving average to keep responsiveness to real regressions.\",\n    \"2025-02-23: TTL for rollback set to default 1 hour (3600s) with per-project override up to 24h. This prevents thrashing on releases with transient infra noise.\",\n    \"2025-02-27: Add safety profiles to Console UI. Conservative profile uses 2x sensitivity threshold and 15-minute hysteresis; Balanced uses current defaults; Aggressive is for fast iteration only behind manual approval.\",\n    \"2025-03-01: Require a synthetic probe pass (end-to-end) with traffic replay for every canary before crossing 5% traffic in production for Dedicated customers.\"\n  ],\n  \"next_steps\": [\n    \"Merge PR #4821 and rollout to staging cluster behind feature flag (assigned Marcelo).\",\n    \"Add a temporary PagerDuty alert rule for sustained bad_response_rate during canary windows (assigned Lindsey).\",\n    \"Publish Canary Safety Runbook and link checklist to Console promotion flow (assigned Aisha).\",\n    \"Design finalize mockups and handoff to frontend for safety profile selector (assigned Hiro).\",\n    \"Schedule dedicated capacity integration test with customer-rep traffic replay (assigned Priya).\"\n  ],\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"comments\",\n    \"decision_log\",\n    \"next_steps\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_63dc81476f6047fdbdf584c3bcd64f77\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Canary rollout postmortem: automated safety gates, probe hysteresis, and rollback TTLs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-9402-canary-rollback-postmortem-actions-and-safety-automation.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Model-lifecycle-tooling\nTeam: engineering\n\n7124 - eng - 9021 customer impact : high release : runtime - 1. 19 security review required : false description : summary : during a recent canary rollout of model v2. 3 we observed a progressive increase in bad response rates across a small percentage of traffic and an eventual failed auto - rollback because the safety gate hysteresis allowed transient noise to be treated as stable regressions. this ticket captures the postmortem actions and tracks engineering work to harden canary safety gates, add automated sanity - runbooks, and implement a configurable rollback ttl and probe smoothing to avoid flapping.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Canary rollout postmortem: automated safety gates, probe hysteresis, and rollback TTLs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-9402-canary-rollback-postmortem-actions-and-safety-automation.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Model-lifecycle-tooling\nTeam: engineering\n\n- 2025 - 02 - 20 — aisha patel : filed after incident inc - 2025 - 112. initial triage : regression signature was 0. 8 % bad _ response _ rate at 3 % traffic increasing to 2. 6 % over 30 minutes. canary controller rolled back once then failed to re - promote ; logs show hysteresis window configured at 5 minutes which allowed noisy spike to be interpreted as sustained regression. - 2025 - 02 - 21 — marcelo ruiz : reproduced locally with traffic replay. root cause appears to be twofold : ( 1 ) probe smoothing configured as simple moving average with short window ; ( 2 ) rollback policy lacks ttl so subsequent canary promotions immediately retriggered the same checks.",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Canary rollout postmortem: automated safety gates, probe hysteresis, and rollback TTLs\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/linear\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-9402-canary-rollback-postmortem-actions-and-safety-automation.json\nConnector: linear\nWorkspace: engineering\nProject: Model-lifecycle-tooling\nTeam: engineering\n\n- 2025 - 02 - 22 : agreed to implement exponential smoothing ( configurable alpha ) rather than longer simple moving average to keep responsiveness to real regressions. - 2025 - 02 - 23 : ttl for rollback set to default 1 hour ( 3600s ) with per - project override up to 24h. this prevents thrashing on releases with transient infra noise. - 2025 - 02 - 27 : add safety profiles to console ui. conservative profile uses 2x sensitivity threshold and 15 - minute hysteresis ; balanced uses current defaults ; aggressive is for fast iteration only behind manual approval. - 2025 - 03 - 01 : require a synthetic probe pass ( end - to - end )",

document.title: Canary rollout postmortem: automated safety gates, probe hysteresis, and rollback TTLs
document.content:
{
  "key": "ENG-9402",
  "team": "engineering",
  "title": "Canary rollout postmortem: automated safety gates, probe hysteresis, and rollback TTLs",
  "status": "In Progress",
  "priority": "P0",
  "created_at": "2025-02-20",
  "updated_at": "2025-03-05",
  "creator": "Aisha Patel",
  "assignee": "Marcelo Ruiz",
  "project": "Model-lifecycle-tooling",
  "cycle": "2025-W08",
  "estimate": "5",
  "due_date": "2025-03-12",
  "labels": [
    "canary-rollout",
    "postmortem",
    "auto-rollback",
    "observability",
    "runbook"
  ],
  "parent_issue": [
    "ENG-8739"
  ],
  "dependencies": [
    "ENG-7124",
    "ENG-9021"
  ],
  "customer_impact": "high",
  "release": "runtime-1.19",
  "security_review_required": "false",
  "description": "Summary: During a recent canary rollout of model v2.3 we observed a progressive increase in bad response rates across a small percentage of traffic and an eventual failed auto-rollback because the safety gate hysteresis allowed transient noise to be treated as stable regressions. This ticket captures the postmortem actions and tracks engineering work to harden canary safety gates, add automated sanity-runbooks, and implement a configurable rollback TTL and probe smoothing to avoid flapping.\n\nGoals: \n- Collect incident learnings and formalize them into a canary safety runbook.\n- Implement probe hysteresis and exponential backoff to reduce false positives from transient spikes.\n- Add a rollback TTL and a circuit-breaker to prevent repeated rollbacks within short windows.\n- Create automated canary dashboards and alert thresholds tied to traffic-weighted metrics.\n- Add an audit log and post-deploy checklist that must pass before canary promotes beyond 5% traffic.\n\nScope: runtime canary controller, Redwood Console rollout UI, alerting rules in PagerDuty/Dashboards, runbook docs, and a follow-up QA pass on dedicated capacity behavior.\n\nSuccess criteria: \n- New runbook published to Confluence with a clear escalation path and playbook steps.\n- Canary controller implements smoothing and rollback TTL (configurable per-release).\n- Observability dashboards with synthetic probe traces and traffic-weighted SLOs available in staging and production.\n- One simulated canary test with injected faults runs cleanly (no false rollback) before rollout to customers.\n\nNotes: This is time-sensitive because the customer who triggered the incident is on a dedicated capacity contract and expects a write-up plus mitigations within 2 weeks.",
  "comments": [
    "2025-02-20 \u2014 Aisha Patel: Filed after incident INC-2025-112. Initial triage: regression signature was 0.8% bad_response_rate at 3% traffic increasing to 2.6% over 30 minutes. Canary controller rolled back once then failed to re-promote; logs show hysteresis window configured at 5 minutes which allowed noisy spike to be interpreted as sustained regression.",
    "2025-02-21 \u2014 Marcelo Ruiz: Reproduced locally with traffic replay. Root cause appears to be twofold: (1) probe smoothing configured as simple moving average with short window; (2) rollback policy lacks TTL so subsequent canary promotions immediately retriggered the same checks. Drafting patch for smoothing and TTL config in canary controller.",
    "2025-02-24 \u2014 SRE Review (Lindsey Wong): Recommended adding median-based probe plus percentile trimming to avoid outlier-driven signals. Also suggested a temporary alert to page on 1.5% sustained bad_response_rate over 20 minutes during canary windows.",
    "2025-02-27 \u2014 Design (Hiro Tanaka): Console UX update: expose a 'safety profile' selector (conservative, balanced, aggressive) with defaults and per-release overrides. Planned mockups linked.",
    "2025-03-02 \u2014 Marcelo Ruiz: Draft PR submitted implementing exponential smoothing (alpha configurable) and rollback_ttl_seconds with default 3600s. PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4821",
    "2025-03-04 \u2014 QA (Priya Desai): Ran canary simulation with injected 0.5% latency noise and 2x error spikes for 3 minutes \u2014 no false positive rollback after smoothing enabled; TTL prevented immediate re-rollouts. Pending integration tests in dedicated capacity environment."
  ],
  "attachments": [
    "Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/Canary+Safety+Runbook",
    "Incident: INC-2025-112 (internal) https://redwood.incidents/INC-2025-112",
    "GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4821",
    "Dashboard (staging): https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/rollouts/canary-health?orgId=1"
  ],
  "decision_log": [
    "2025-02-22: Agreed to implement exponential smoothing (configurable alpha) rather than longer simple moving average to keep responsiveness to real regressions.",
    "2025-02-23: TTL for rollback set to default 1 hour (3600s) with per-project override up to 24h. This prevents thrashing on releases with transient infra noise.",
    "2025-02-27: Add safety profiles to Console UI. Conservative profile uses 2x sensitivity threshold and 15-minute hysteresis; Balanced uses current defaults; Aggressive is for fast iteration only behind manual approval.",
    "2025-03-01: Require a synthetic probe pass (end-to-end) with traffic replay for every canary before crossing 5% traffic in production for Dedicated customers."
  ],
  "next_steps": [
    "Merge PR #4821 and rollout to staging cluster behind feature flag (assigned Marcelo).",
    "Add a temporary PagerDuty alert rule for sustained bad_response_rate during canary windows (assigned Lindsey).",
    "Publish Canary Safety Runbook and link checklist to Console promotion flow (assigned Aisha).",
    "Design finalize mockups and handoff to frontend for safety profile selector (assigned Hiro).",
    "Schedule dedicated capacity integration test with customer-rep traffic replay (assigned Priya)."
  ],
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "description",
    "comments",
    "decision_log",
    "next_steps"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_63dc81476f6047fdbdf584c3bcd64f77"
}

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_46a4d80929554f98bdec1f3f63f3e9eb",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/fireflies/customer-success/2025-03-12-acme-ai-incident-review-and-diagnostics-gaps.json",
    "title": "Acme AI - incident review + diagnostics gaps (deploy/config/saturation)",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/fireflies",
    "content": "{
  "meeting_id": "ff-20250312-acmeai-incident-review-7f3c1b",
  "recorded_at": "2025-03-12T17:03:14-07:00",
  "duration_minutes": "54",
  "call_type": "technical_deep_dive",
  "title": "Acme AI - incident review + diagnostics gaps (deploy/config/saturation)",
  "redwood_owner": "Dev Patel",
  "redwood_attendees": [
    "Dev Patel",
    "Owen Phillips",
    "Miles Thornton",
    "Jacob Stein",
    "Logan Wright"
  ],
  "customer_company": "Acme AI",
  "customer_attendees": [
    "Sarah Kim (Head of Platform Engineering)",
    "Miguel Alvarez (SRE)",
    "Anika Rao (ML Platform)",
    "Jordan Price (Staff Backend Engineer)",
    "Elaine Chen (Security & Compliance)"
  ],
  "crm_account_id": "CRM-ACCT-008241",
  "competitors_mentioned": [
    "AWS Bedrock",
    "Anyscale",
    "OpenAI"
  ],
  "transcription_quality": "medium",
  "summary": "Acme AI walked Redwood through the 3/10 incident impact (p95 latency spike + intermittent 503s on a subset of routes) and the biggest diagnostic gaps: (1) no easy \u201cwhat deployed recently\u201d context tied to the incident thread, (2) config/routing changes were hard to confirm quickly and safely (feature flags, model pins, quota/rate-limit) without manually paging multiple teams, and (3) saturation signals were inconsistent (GPU util looked fine, but queue depth + KV cache pressure were elevated). Redwood shared planned Incident Bot v2 context cards (recent deploys, tenant-safe config diffs with redaction, saturation signals + deep links), plus constraints around permissioning/audit logging and query budgets. Agreed on a short beta for Acme\u2019s on-call runbooks and which dashboards/links would be most useful.",

  "summary": "Acme AI walked Redwood through the 3/10 incident impact (p95 latency spike + intermittent 503s on a subset of routes) and the biggest diagnostic gaps: (1) no easy “what deployed recently” context tied to the incident thread, (2) config/routing changes were hard to confirm quickly and safely (feature flags, model pins, quota/rate-limit) without manually paging multiple teams, and (3) saturation signals were inconsistent (GPU util looked fine, but queue depth + KV cache pressure were elevated). Redwood shared planned Incident Bot v2 context cards (recent deploys, tenant-safe config diffs with redaction, saturation signals + deep links), plus constraints around permissioning/audit logging and query budgets. Agreed on a short beta for Acme’s on-call runbooks and which dashboards/links would be most useful.",
  "topics": [
    "Incident recap: symptoms, blast radius, and timeline gaps",
    "Deploy context: service/version, canary vs full rollout, links to PR/commit",
    "Config diff needs: feature flags, routing policy, quota changes, model pins; redaction + audit",
    "Saturation signals: GPU util vs queue depth vs KV cache pressure; regional capacity and backpressure",
    "Deep links: console dashboards, traces/log correlation, error budget burn views",
    "Beta/rollout plan for Incident Bot v2 and success criteria (time-to-triage, completeness)"
  ],
  "action_items": [
    "Dev Patel - Send Acme the incident timeline export + preliminary root cause notes (by 2025-03-13)",
    "Jacob Stein - Share sample Incident Bot v2 context card screenshots (deploy/config/sat) and get feedback on what to prioritize (by 2025-03-14)",
    "Logan Wright - Confirm which saturation metrics are available tenant-safely for Acme’s dedicated pool (queue depth, admission control, KV cache pressure) and recommended thresholds (by 2025-03-18)",
    "Miles Thornton - Add Acme-specific deep link parameters (service/region/time window) to the bot card link templates (by 2025-03-20)",
    "Elaine Chen (Acme) - Provide Acme’s security requirements for audit log retention + who can access config diffs during incidents (by 2025-03-19)",

  ],
  "next_steps": [

    "Redwood to provide a one-pager on the diagnostic signals: definitions, what’s actionable, and links to dashboards."
  ],
  "transcript": "Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: Acme AI - incident review + diagnostics gaps (deploy/config/saturation)
Date: 2025-03-12
Time: 5:03 PM - 5:57 PM (PT)
Duration: 54 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dev Patel, Owen Phillips, Miles Thornton, Jacob Stein, Logan Wright
Acme AI: Sarah Kim, Miguel Alvarez, Anika Rao, Jordan Price, Elaine Chen

Auto-summary (generated)
- Acme described the incident as “slow then spiky”: p95 latency rose first, then bursts of 503s.
- Biggest pain: responders couldn’t quickly answer “what changed” (deploys + config) and “are we saturated” (queue/KV pressure) from one place.
- Redwood reviewed Incident Bot v2 direction: deploy context card, tenant-safe config diffs with redaction + audit logs, and saturation signals with bounded queries + cached fallback.

Questions (captured)
- Can the bot show canary status and rollout phase, not just a SHA?
- Can config diff be scoped to only the tenant-safe keys and still be useful?
- Which saturation signals are most actionable for Acme: GPU util, queue depth, KV cache pressure, or scheduler backpressure?
- How will deep links land in the right region/time window during an active incident?

Action items (captured)
- Redwood to send timeline + card mockups.
- Redwood to validate saturation metric availability for Acme’s pool.
- Acme security to confirm access policy + audit retention needs.

---

[00:00] Dev Patel: Okay, cool. Folks are in. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Dev from Redwood, I run the support escalation side. Goal today is… not to relive the pain too much, but to understand what was missing for you in the first like five, ten minutes.

[00:18] Sarah Kim: Yeah. Appreciate you all jumping on. For context, this was Monday for us, 3/10. We had like elevated p95 and then some intermittent 503s on our chat completion route.

[00:29] Owen Phillips: Owen here, I’m CS on the account. I’ll mostly listen, but yeah, we want to make sure we fix the “day two ops” stuff, not just this one incident.

[00:39] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel, I’m the SRE on call that day. I’ll be blunt—our first 20 minutes were basically Slack archeology.

[00:48] (crosstalk)

[00:50] Dev Patel: That’s fair. Maybe we start with a quick timeline from your side, Miguel, then we’ll drill into the diagnostics gaps. Sound good?

[01:00] Miguel Alvarez: Yep. So around 10:12 AM Pacific we got a latency page. Not like total outage, but p95 went from ~650ms to like 1.8 seconds on one of the primary routes. Then at 10:18-ish we start seeing 503s, but only in bursts.

[01:18] Miguel Alvarez: Our first question was, “did Redwood deploy something,” because the shape looked like a regression. We asked in the shared channel, but we didn’t have anything in the incident thread that said “here are recent deploys for serving-api in us-west” or whatever.

[01:34] Sarah Kim: And separately, we had made a routing policy tweak earlier that morning. Minor. But we couldn’t quickly confirm whether it had fully propagated or whether it overlapped with Redwood changes.

[01:49] Jacob Stein: Jacob, I’m on diagnostics tooling. When you say routing policy tweak, is that like model pin, or traffic split, or…?

[01:56] Sarah Kim: For us it was a traffic split between two model variants. We were trying to roll back a quant profile—sorry, I don’t remember your exact term. We basically adjusted the fallback chain.

[02:10] Jacob Stein: Got it. That’s exactly the kind of thing we want to surface safely.

[02:15] Dev Patel: And then saturation—did you suspect capacity right away, or did it look more like errors?

[02:22] Miguel Alvarez: Initially we thought saturation, because latency rose first. But the GPU utilization dashboard we have access to looked… fine? Like 60-65%. Which was confusing.

[02:33] Anika Rao: Yeah, and we were looking at tokens per second and it dropped, but not in a way that screamed “no capacity.” More like queueing.

[02:43] Logan Wright: Logan from telemetry. That “GPU util looks fine but everything is slow” is classic queue depth / KV cache pressure territory. Depending on batching/backpressure, you can have headroom on raw GPU while the scheduler is choking.

[03:00] Jordan Price: Jordan, backend. The other issue was we had to open like three different tools. One dashboard for GPU, another for request errors, and then we were asking your team for “what changed.” It’s just not one workflow.

[03:16] Dev Patel: Yep. So that’s basically the project we’re doing internally—Incident Bot v2—push the “what changed” plus “are we saturated” into the incident thread automatically.

[03:27] Elaine Chen: Before we go too far, Elaine from security. When you say “push into the thread,” does that include tenant configuration? Because that’s sensitive on our side.

[03:36] Miles Thornton: Miles here, I own incident automation. Great question. The plan is a tenant-safe config diff: allowlist keys, redact anything that looks like a secret, and emit audit log events any time the bot fetches it. We can also restrict who can expand details.

[03:55] Elaine Chen: Okay. We’ll need to understand retention on the audit logs and who the “break glass” approver is.

[04:02] Dev Patel: Totally. We’ll come back to that. Miguel, can you describe the moment you felt blocked?

[04:10] Miguel Alvarez: Honestly right after the initial page. We posted “any deploys?” and we waited. Meanwhile we’re trying to decide: do we fail over regions? do we reduce max tokens? We didn’t know if we were in a canary or full rollout.

[04:28] Miguel Alvarez: If we had a card that said “Serving API deployed 17 minutes ago, phase: 20% canary, canary error rate elevated,” we would’ve immediately frozen changes and focused on rollback.

[04:44] Jacob Stein: That’s helpful. So the deploy card needs: service, version/SHA, rollout phase, and canary health summary. Plus links to PR/commit.

[04:55] Sarah Kim: Yeah, and ideally scope it to the region. Because “a deploy happened somewhere” isn’t useful.

[05:03] Logan Wright: Region scoping is doable as long as we can map deploy events to the serving pools. That’s work we’re mid-flight on.

[05:13] Dev Patel: On the config side, what would have saved you time?

[05:18] Sarah Kim: A diff. Like, “routing policy changed at 09:47 by Sarah, changed fallback order A->B to A->C” and “quota changed” kind of thing.

[05:30] Sarah Kim: We had to go into our internal change log plus your console plus ask support. And we still weren’t sure if it propagated.

[05:40] Jordan Price: And the feature flags. I don’t know if you call them flags or toggles, but we needed to know if something flipped.

[05:47] Miles Thornton: Internally we call them feature flags and policy toggles. The planned config diff card includes: feature flags, routing policy, quota/rate limit, and model pins. The key is redaction: we don’t want to leak prompts, customer IDs, anything like that.

[06:05] Elaine Chen: Also, we don’t want config diffs dumped into a big shared Slack where not all participants are authorized.

[06:12] Owen Phillips: Understood. For most customers we keep incident channels limited, but we can also have the bot post a summary and require an interaction to view more.

[06:23] Jacob Stein: Like “Diff available: 12 changes, 4 redacted,” then click to open a modal if you have permission.

[06:31] Elaine Chen: That’s the right pattern.

[06:34] Dev Patel: Switching to saturation signals—what did you wish you saw beyond GPU util?

[06:41] Miguel Alvarez: Queue depth per region. Something that says “requests are stacking up.”

[06:47] Anika Rao: KV cache pressure, if you have it. We saw longer sequences during that window, and I suspect it blew out cache.

[06:55] Logan Wright: We do have KV cache metrics, but sometimes the label cardinality explodes if we do it wrong. We’re standardizing it. The bot will show a summary: “KV cache pressure high” with a link to the dashboard rather than raw per-model lines.

[07:13] Jordan Price: And ideally also “scheduler backpressure.” We kept hearing that term from your support during the incident, but we couldn’t see it.

[07:22] Logan Wright: Yep. We call it admission control / backpressure indicators. The bot card for saturation is planned to include: GPU utilization, queue depth, scheduler saturation, and KV cache pressure. Plus a quick “likely cause” hint, but we’ll be careful not to over-automate guesses.

[07:42] Dev Patel: Let’s talk about the deep links. During the incident, what did you click most?

[07:48] Miguel Alvarez: Traces. But we didn’t have the trace link that was already scoped to the time window.

[07:55] Sarah Kim: We also wanted a “dashboard bundle” link. One click to open the right service, right region, last 30 minutes.

[08:05] Miles Thornton: That’s in scope: links into Console dashboards and trace/log correlation links. The trick is making sure it lands correctly and doesn’t time out.

[08:17] Jacob Stein: Also, if upstream telemetry is slow during an incident, the bot should degrade to cached context + links rather than hanging.

[08:27] Miguel Alvarez: That would be huge. We had your dashboards go sluggish while we were trying to debug, which is kind of ironic.

[08:36] Logan Wright: Yeah, that’s a known failure mode. We’re adding caching and query budgets so the bot doesn’t DoS the metrics system.

[08:46] Dev Patel: For the record, during Monday we also saw a telemetry query latency spike. That’s on us.

[08:53] Sarah Kim: Understood. We just want predictable “first five minutes” data.

[09:00] Dev Patel: Okay. I’m going to sanity-check what I heard:
- Card 1: Recent deploys with canary health, per service/region, link to PR.
- Card 2: Config diff with redaction, propagation hints, and audit.
- Card 3: Saturation signals beyond GPU util: queue depth, KV pressure, scheduler/backpressure.
Plus deep links and degraded mode.

[09:23] Sarah Kim: Yes.

[09:24] Miguel Alvarez: And one more—some indication of “regional capacity constraints.” Like, is us-east out of headroom? Because we were debating failover.

[09:34] Logan Wright: That’s part of the regional capacity signal. We can show “capacity tight” per pool, but again, summarized.

[09:43] Anika Rao: Also, if you show that, it should include whether fallback routing is active. Because our traffic might be shifted without us realizing.

[09:53] Jacob Stein: That ties into routing policy context. We can include “fallback engaged” and “model variant” changes.

[10:04] Elaine Chen: Quick question on the config diff: will it show the actor? Like, who changed it?

[10:09] Miles Thornton: Where it’s our control plane changes, yes, we can show “changed by” if it’s a Redwood operator or an automated rollout. For customer-initiated changes, we can show the principal if your identity is federated. If not, it may be an API key name.

[10:26] Elaine Chen: Okay. Just make sure it doesn’t expose secrets. API key names are fine.

[10:31] Dev Patel: On the incident itself—do you want to walk through the root cause we found, or keep this focused on diagnostics needs?

[10:39] Sarah Kim: We can do five minutes on cause, but the bigger value is the tooling. We already got the post-incident note.

[10:47] Dev Patel: Got it. Very quick: there was a deploy affecting request scheduling logic in one region. It increased queueing under certain sequence length distributions. That’s why GPU didn’t look pegged.

[11:05] Miguel Alvarez: That matches what we saw. Okay.

[11:08] Jordan Price: So that deploy card would have basically told us “scheduling changed,” yeah?

[11:13] Jacob Stein: It would at least tell you “a deploy happened.” We’re also exploring attaching “related PRs” and a short change summary, but we need to make sure it’s accurate.

[11:27] Owen Phillips: And to be clear, this is not just for Redwood-internal incidents. We want it to help your on-call too.

[11:35] Sarah Kim: Right. Our on-call needs to know: do we roll back our routing change, or is Redwood rolling something back.

[11:44] Dev Patel: On the beta: we’re planning a feature-flagged rollout. Would Acme be open to being a design partner? Basically you’d see the cards in your incident threads and we’d iterate.

[11:57] Sarah Kim: Yes, with two caveats: security sign-off on config diff access, and we don’t want additional noise.

[12:06] Miguel Alvarez: And it can’t slow down response. If the bot posts 30 seconds later than the page, it’s still useful, but if it’s like 10 minutes later, no.

[12:16] Miles Thornton: Understood. We’re targeting sub-60 seconds for the first post, with cached follow-ups.

[12:25] Logan Wright: And we’ll cap query cost. Under high load it will fall back to links.

[12:33] Elaine Chen: How do you handle audit logs? Like, if someone expands a config diff, does that get logged?

[12:40] Miles Thornton: Yes. “Bot accessed config diff” plus “user requested expanded view” are separate audit events. They go to our SIEM pipeline. We can share retention defaults and options.

[12:55] Elaine Chen: We’ll want at least 1 year retention.

[12:58] Owen Phillips: Noted.

[13:01] Dev Patel: Let’s go deeper on what “config diff” means for you. Sarah, what objects would you want included?

[13:08] Sarah Kim: Routing policy, model pins, rate limits, and any rollout toggles. If you can also show “last updated timestamp” that would be great.

[13:20] Jordan Price: And it should show if the change partially applied. We’ve had cases where a policy is updated but only in one region.

[13:28] Jacob Stein: That’s the “partial propagation” problem. We can include a propagation status if the control plane has it. Otherwise we can at least show “observed config version” per region.

[13:45] Logan Wright: From telemetry, we can sometimes infer it by seeing the policy version label—again, careful about cardinality.

[13:54] Miguel Alvarez: Even a hint would help. Our team spent time arguing whether the change “took.”

[14:03] Dev Patel: On saturation thresholds—what would you want the bot to highlight? Like, should it say “red” at queue depth > X?

[14:12] Miguel Alvarez: We’d like “this is unusual compared to baseline,” not just a fixed number. But we’ll take fixed if that’s all.

[14:23] Logan Wright: We can do both. For the card, likely: fixed threshold + delta vs 7-day baseline. But we have to keep it simple.

[14:34] Anika Rao: For KV cache pressure, can you translate it into “you’re evicting” or “cache hit rate dropped”?

[14:40] Logan Wright: Yeah, we track eviction rate and hit ratio. The bot can say “KV evictions elevated” which is more actionable.

[14:51] Jordan Price: Actionable means “reduce max tokens” or “change batching,” right?

[14:56] Jacob Stein: Exactly, and the bot can link to the runbook. We’re updating runbooks so responders don’t guess.

[15:06] Miguel Alvarez: If the bot said “KV evictions high; mitigation: reduce context length or lower concurrency,” that’s already helpful.

[15:16] Miles Thornton: We’ll probably keep the card to: signal + link to runbook, to avoid bad automation. But we can include a short “common mitigations” snippet.

[15:28] Dev Patel: Let’s touch on deep links again. Jordan, what did you want as a single click?

[15:34] Jordan Price: A link that opens the dashboard with the right filters. We kept losing time typing region/service filters.

[15:44] Owen Phillips: Like a permalink with service=acme-chat, region=us-west2, time=last_30m.

[15:50] Sarah Kim: Exactly.

[15:52] Logan Wright: Also for traces, we can embed a pre-filtered trace explorer link. There’s some auth constraints but doable.

[16:02] Elaine Chen: As long as it respects RBAC.

[16:05] Logan Wright: Yes, it goes through the same auth.

[16:10] Dev Patel: I want to capture one more pain point: during Monday, did you feel you had to ask Redwood engineers for basic facts?

[16:18] Miguel Alvarez: Yes. We asked “is there a deploy” and “what’s the current canary” and “is there capacity.” That’s not a criticism, but it’s a lot of back-and-forth.

[16:31] Sarah Kim: And it’s not scalable if we’re going to run more workloads on you.

[16:36] Dev Patel: Agreed.

[16:38] Jacob Stein: One design question: would you prefer one big post or multiple cards?

[16:44] Miguel Alvarez: Multiple cards. Big posts get ignored.

[16:49] Sarah Kim: Yeah, three cards max, then drill-down.

[16:53] Miles Thornton: That matches our plan: Deploy / Config / Saturation. Plus a small “links” footer.

[17:02] Anika Rao: And maybe “error budget burn” if you have it.

[17:06] Dev Patel: We do have an error budget view internally. For customers, we can at least show the SLO burn rate chart link. We’ll see what we can expose.

[17:17] Owen Phillips: We’ve been discussing a “SLO toolkit” link generator. That’s coming.

[17:23] Sarah Kim: Good.

[17:25] Elaine Chen: Can we talk about who can see config diffs? On our side, we’d like only platform on-call and security, not every developer.

[17:35] Miles Thornton: We can map that via Slack user groups + bot scopes. For example, the bot posts a summary, but “View diff” is only enabled for an allowed group.

[17:48] Elaine Chen: And if someone outside that group tries?

[17:51] Miles Thornton: They get a message like “Insufficient permissions; request access,” and it’s logged.

[17:58] Elaine Chen: Perfect.

[18:01] Dev Patel: Switching gears: were there any false leads because of missing saturation signals?

[18:07] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, because GPU util was moderate, we assumed it wasn’t capacity, so we looked at network. But later it was basically queueing.

[18:17] Logan Wright: That’s why we want queue depth and scheduler saturation in the card. GPU util alone is misleading.

[18:26] Jordan Price: Also, our team debated whether to shift traffic to eu-west because we saw errors in us-west. If we had known eu-west was already tight, we wouldn’t.

[18:38] Logan Wright: Regional capacity signal can prevent that.

[18:41] Sarah Kim: Yep.

[18:43] Dev Patel: Okay. I think we have enough on requirements. Let’s outline the beta.

[18:50] Owen Phillips: Proposal: once we have the cards stable, we enable for Acme-prod incidents only, in two regions, for one on-call rotation. You give us feedback.

[19:03] Miguel Alvarez: Works.

[19:05] Sarah Kim: How soon?

[19:07] Miles Thornton: We’re aiming end of March for broader beta, but we can share mockups this week and confirm what you want before we flip anything.

[19:18] Jacob Stein: I can send screenshots of card layouts and sample redaction warnings.

[19:25] Elaine Chen: Please do. Especially the redaction behavior.

[19:29] Dev Patel: Logan, can you validate which saturation metrics we can expose safely to Acme? Specifically KV cache pressure and scheduler backpressure.

[19:38] Logan Wright: Yep. For dedicated pools, we should have them. I’ll confirm label set and ensure it’s tenant-safe.

[19:48] Anika Rao: What does “tenant-safe” mean here exactly?

[19:52] Logan Wright: Basically: the metric query only returns your tenant’s data, and the labels don’t include things that identify other tenants. Also we avoid raw per-request IDs.

[20:06] Anika Rao: Great.

[20:08] Jordan Price: Can the bot also show “queue depth at router” versus “queue depth at scheduler”? Because those mean different things.

[20:16] Logan Wright: We likely show one combined “effective queue depth” plus a drill-down link. Too much detail in the card gets confusing.

[20:26] Miguel Alvarez: Agreed. Keep the card short.

[20:29] Dev Patel: Elaine, you mentioned audit retention. Can you send your requirements? One year, anything else?

[20:36] Elaine Chen: One year, searchable by user and by incident ID. And we’ll need to know if you can export to us or at least provide reports.

[20:48] Owen Phillips: We can provide audit reports as part of the enterprise support package. Let’s follow up offline.

[20:55] Dev Patel: Cool.

[20:56] (brief pause)

[21:00] Sarah Kim: One more request—during incidents, we often ask “what changed in the last hour.” Can the bot automatically include a one-hour window for deploys and config?

[21:10] Jacob Stein: Yes. The default is “last 60 minutes” and we can let you expand to 6 hours.

[21:17] Miguel Alvarez: That’s good. Don’t go beyond that by default.

[21:22] Miles Thornton: And we’ll include timestamps in UTC and local? Or just UTC?

[21:28] Miguel Alvarez: UTC is fine, but be consistent.

[21:31] Dev Patel: Noted.

[21:34] Jordan Price: Also, can the bot include “known ongoing incident” banner? Like if Redwood already has a regional issue.

[21:43] Owen Phillips: We can include a link to our status page and internal incident ID if there is one. But we’re not overhauling status tooling as part of this.

[21:54] Sarah Kim: Even a link is fine.

[21:57] Dev Patel: Okay.

[22:00] Miguel Alvarez: I want to make sure you heard the key pain: we couldn’t decide between mitigation options because we didn’t know whether it was deploy regression, our config, or saturation.

[22:12] Dev Patel: Heard loud and clear. That’s literally the three cards.

[22:17] Jacob Stein: Quick check—would you want the bot to recommend “rollback deploy” vs “rollback config”? Or just present evidence?

[22:25] Sarah Kim: Evidence. Recommendations are risky.

[22:28] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah, just evidence.

[22:31] Logan Wright: We can highlight anomalies without prescribing.

[22:35] Dev Patel: Good.

[22:37] (crosstalk)

[22:40] Dev Patel: Anything else we missed?

[22:44] Anika Rao: Minor: include “streaming disconnects” metric if applicable. We saw some client-side drops.

[22:52] Logan Wright: That’s part of the SLO signal set. We can link to the streaming health dashboard.

[22:58] Jordan Price: Great.

[23:00] Dev Patel: Okay, we’ll do a quick recap and then give you time back.

[23:06] Dev Patel: Next steps: I’ll send the incident timeline export tomorrow. Jacob sends card mockups by Friday. Logan confirms saturation metrics availability and thresholds next week. Miles updates link templates.

[23:21] Dev Patel: Elaine, you send audit/access requirements and we’ll align on the permission model.

[23:28] Elaine Chen: Yes.

[23:30] Sarah Kim: Sounds good. Thanks all.

[23:33] Miguel Alvarez: Thanks. Looking forward to not doing Slack archeology next time.

[23:39] Owen Phillips: Same. Appreciate the candor.

    "content": "{\n  \"thread_id\": \"thread-20271201-karthik-nimbus-dr-sla\",\n  \"mailbox_owner\": \"karthik_iyer\",\n  \"subject\": \"Regional availability carve-out and staged failover proposal for Nimbus Health\",\n  \"participants_internal\": [\n    \"Karthik Iyer\",\n    \"Lauren Bishop\",\n    \"Ben Carter\",\n    \"Neha Kapoor\"\n  ],\n  \"participants_external\": [\n    \"Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>\",\n    \"Nimbus Health Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>\",\n    \"Aria Gomez <aria.gomez@nimbushealth.com>\"\n  ],\n  \"message_count\": \"5\",\n  \"first_email_at\": \"2027-12-01T09:12:00-08:00\",\n  \"last_email_at\": \"2027-12-03T09:00:00-08:00\",\n  \"thread_type\": \"procurement\",\n  \"related_account\": \"Nimbus Health\",\n  \"deal_id\": \"NBH-2027-Q4-57\",\n  \"region\": \"us\",\n  \"has_attachments\": \"true\",\n  \"attachments\": [\n    \"redwood-staged-failover-proposal.pdf\",\n    \"nimbus-requested-sla-draft.docx\"\n  ],\n  \"related_links\": [\n    \"https://redwood.app/drive/proposals/NBH-2027-Q4-57\",\n    \"DocuSign: 0a9f-ndk-229\"\n  ],\n  \"messages\": [\n    \"From: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>\\nTo: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>\\nCc: Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>\\nDate: 2027-12-01T09:12:00-08:00\\nSubject: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows\\n\\nHi Karthik,\\n\\nThanks again for the demo last week. We're moving toward a production pilot for patient-facing summaries and need to lock down availability guarantees before procurement can sign off. Nimbus' security and ops teams have a hard requirement for multi-region failover across US-EAST and US-WEST with the following asks:\\n\\n- RTO <= 5 minutes for stateless API requests on failover\\n- RPO = 0 for telemetry and audit logs (no loss)\\n- Maintain 99.9% request success across regions; 99th percentile latency <= 300ms under normal operation\\n\\nWe understand there are trade-offs; please confirm whether Redwood can commit to these in the Enterprise SOW or whether an exception/carveout is required. If a carveout is necessary, we need the alternate SLOs plus remediation and credit language to move forward.\\n\\nAttached is a redlined SOW template for reference.\\n\\nAppreciate a quick turnaround \\u2014 procurement is targeting next-week approval.\\n\\nRegards,\\nJasdeep\\nDirector of IT Operations\\nNimbus Health\\n\\nAttachment: nimbus-requested-sla-draft.docx (docx, 360KB)\",\n    \"From: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>\\nTo: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>\\nCc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>\\nDate: 2027-12-01T12:45:00-05:00\\nSubject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows\\n\\nJasdeep \\u2014\\n\\nThanks for the clear asks and the SOW. Short answer: we can meet the stateless API RTO target in most cases but we cannot guarantee RPO=0 for telemetry and audit logs without specific replication plumbing in your architecture. A few quick points and a proposed staged alternative:\\n\\n1) Stateless API RTO: For purely stateless calls (no session KV), our multi-region warm standby + automated DNS failover can deliver failover detection and routing in ~30\\u201390s; full capacity recovery to 95% depends on model warmup and cache state. We can commit to an RTO target of <=3 minutes for the ingress routing and <=15 minutes for full throughput recovery for a standard Dedicated configuration.\\n\\n2) Stateful/KV-backed requests & RPO: We do not provide synchronous cross-region write replication by default. Audit/telemetry with RPO=0 would require either: synchronous replication to a customer-managed replica (recommended), or Redwood-managed active-active session replication (extra-cost add-on). Without that, worst-case RPO for in-flight KV writes during a region outage is non-zero; we typically size this at an expected window of up to 5 minutes for write buffers that haven't been flushed.\\n\\n3) Latency SLOs: Our 99th percentile latency across regional endpoints is normally <= 300ms for supported models and standard token budgets. During failover we expect elevated latencies; proposal below captures that.\\n\\nProposed staged failover carveout (for SOW):\\n- Detection & routing: <= 90s\\n- Stateless API RTO (warm routing + partial capacity): <= 3 minutes (95th percentile of simulated events)\\n- Full capacity recovery (including model warmup, KV cache rebuild): <= 15 minutes\\n- RPO for telemetry/audit without synchronous replication: best effort; typical window <= 5 minutes. If RPO=0 is contractually required, Redwood will include an add-on for synchronous replication with architecture work and a 6\\u20138 week delivery timeline.\\n\\nWe can include credits if we miss the staged targets (credit table in attached PDF). I've summarized this in the attached proposal.\\n\\nWould you be available for a short call today to walk procurement through the trade-offs?\\n\\nThanks,\\nKarthik Iyer\\nHead of Sales Engineering\\nRedwood Inference\\n\\nAttachment: redwood-staged-failover-proposal.pdf (pdf, 85KB)\",\n    \"From: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>\\nTo: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>\\nCc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.ai>\\nDate: 2027-12-01T15:00:00-08:00\\nSubject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows\\n\\nJasdeep \\u2014 looping in Legal and Solutions so we can operationalize the carveout cleanly. Two quick clarifications that will shape the SOW language:\\n\\n- Scope: Are you intending Redwood to manage audit/telemetry storage (we host) or will you be pushing telemetry to your managed store? If you host, we can implement synchronous replication options. If you host, our recommended pattern is pushing telemetry via Kafka/Firehose where you own replication semantics.\\n- Acceptable fallback latency: is an elevated latency of up to 700ms P99 during failover acceptable for client UX, given a short period while caches and model quantization warm?\\n\\nBen \\u2014 can you validate how Dedicated config + model pinning affects cold-start time assumptions? Neha \\u2014 please call out any security/compliance notes if we recommend a replication add-on.\\n\\nLauren Bishop\\nVP, Customer Success\\nRedwood Inference\\n\",\n    \"From: Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>\\nTo: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>\\nCc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.ai>, Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>\\nDate: 2027-12-02T10:30:00-08:00\\nSubject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows\\n\\nJasdeep \\u2014 following up with concrete numbers from infra:\\n\\n- Warm standby + sticky KV: typical DNS failover + routing = 30\\u201390s. For endpoints that are purely stateless we see median RTO ~45s in our last tabletop tests.\\n- Full throughput depends on model size and tokenizer warmup: for our recommended medium-sized LLMs (7B\\u201313B quantized) full throughput for concurrent sessions typically returns within 8\\u201312 minutes, 95th percentile up to 15 minutes.\\n- RPO: audit logs that are persisted to our managed logging tier have near-real-time replication within the same region; cross-region synchronous replication is not currently GA. With the add-on (design/engineering work) we can achieve practical RPO <=1s. Without it, design assumption is potential loss of up to 5 minutes of volatile write buffers.\\n\\nIf Nimbus requires RPO=0 and the synchronous replication add-on we will: 1) scope engineering work, 2) estimate cost and timeline (rough ballpark: $65k engineering + infra delta, 6\\u20138 weeks), and 3) add explicit credit terms in the SOW for staged targets.\\n\\nI'll produce a short amendment template for procurement to review.\\n\\n\\u2014Ben\\nPrincipal Solutions Architect\\nRedwood Inference\\n\",\n    \"From: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>\\nTo: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>\\nCc: Nimbus Health Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>, Aria Gomez <aria.gomez@nimbushealth.com>\\nDate: 2027-12-03T09:00:00-08:00\\nSubject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows\\n\\nThanks \\u2014 that framing helps a lot. Procurement is OK with the staged failover language provided Redwood includes:\\n\\n- A defined add-on path priced/committed in the SOW for synchronous cross-region replication to achieve RPO=0 (approximate numbers are acceptable in the amendment)\\n- Credit table tied to the staged targets you listed (detection, stateless RTO, full capacity recovery)\\n- A 30-day SLA review window after go-live to validate assumptions and tune replication/caching rules\\n\\nWe can accept a P99 latency up to 700ms during the 15-minute recovery window if credits apply when thresholds are missed. Please send the amendment + redlined SOW and we will route to legal and procurement for signature.\\n\\nI'll expect the draft amendment by EOD tomorrow.\\n\\n-Jasdeep\\nDirector of IT Operations\\nNimbus Health\"\n  ],\n  \"title_field_name\": \"subject\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"messages\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_04a2b39fcb0148e18c60ee0faa837c94\"\n}",

    "From: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>
To: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>
Cc: Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>
Date: 2027-12-01T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows

Hi Karthik,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're moving toward a production pilot for patient-facing summaries and need to lock down availability guarantees before procurement can sign off. Nimbus' security and ops teams have a hard requirement for multi-region failover across US-EAST and US-WEST with the following asks:

- RTO <= 5 minutes for stateless API requests on failover
- RPO = 0 for telemetry and audit logs (no loss)
- Maintain 99.9% request success across regions; 99th percentile latency <= 300ms under normal operation

We understand there are trade-offs; please confirm whether Redwood can commit to these in the Enterprise SOW or whether an exception/carveout is required. If a carveout is necessary, we need the alternate SLOs plus remediation and credit language to move forward.

Attached is a redlined SOW template for reference.

Appreciate a quick turnaround — procurement is targeting next-week approval.

Regards,
Jasdeep
Director of IT Operations
Nimbus Health

Attachment: nimbus-requested-sla-draft.docx (docx, 360KB)",
    "From: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>
To: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-12-01T12:45:00-05:00
Subject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows

Jasdeep —

Thanks for the clear asks and the SOW. Short answer: we can meet the stateless API RTO target in most cases but we cannot guarantee RPO=0 for telemetry and audit logs without specific replication plumbing in your architecture. A few quick points and a proposed staged alternative:

1) Stateless API RTO: For purely stateless calls (no session KV), our multi-region warm standby + automated DNS failover can deliver failover detection and routing in ~30–90s; full capacity recovery to 95% depends on model warmup and cache state. We can commit to an RTO target of <=3 minutes for the ingress routing and <=15 minutes for full throughput recovery for a standard Dedicated configuration.

2) Stateful/KV-backed requests & RPO: We do not provide synchronous cross-region write replication by default. Audit/telemetry with RPO=0 would require either: synchronous replication to a customer-managed replica (recommended), or Redwood-managed active-active session replication (extra-cost add-on). Without that, worst-case RPO for in-flight KV writes during a region outage is non-zero; we typically size this at an expected window of up to 5 minutes for write buffers that haven't been flushed.

3) Latency SLOs: Our 99th percentile latency across regional endpoints is normally <= 300ms for supported models and standard token budgets. During failover we expect elevated latencies; proposal below captures that.

Proposed staged failover carveout (for SOW):
- Detection & routing: <= 90s
- Stateless API RTO (warm routing + partial capacity): <= 3 minutes (95th percentile of simulated events)
- Full capacity recovery (including model warmup, KV cache rebuild): <= 15 minutes
- RPO for telemetry/audit without synchronous replication: best effort; typical window <= 5 minutes. If RPO=0 is contractually required, Redwood will include an add-on for synchronous replication with architecture work and a 6–8 week delivery timeline.

We can include credits if we miss the staged targets (credit table in attached PDF). I've summarized this in the attached proposal.

Would you be available for a short call today to walk procurement through the trade-offs?

Thanks,
Karthik Iyer
Head of Sales Engineering
Redwood Inference

Attachment: redwood-staged-failover-proposal.pdf (pdf, 85KB)",
    "From: Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>
To: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.ai>
Date: 2027-12-01T15:00:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows

Jasdeep — looping in Legal and Solutions so we can operationalize the carveout cleanly. Two quick clarifications that will shape the SOW language:

- Scope: Are you intending Redwood to manage audit/telemetry storage (we host) or will you be pushing telemetry to your managed store? If you host, we can implement synchronous replication options. If you host, our recommended pattern is pushing telemetry via Kafka/Firehose where you own replication semantics.
- Acceptable fallback latency: is an elevated latency of up to 700ms P99 during failover acceptable for client UX, given a short period while caches and model quantization warm?

Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren@redwood.ai>, Neha Kapoor <neha@redwood.ai>, Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>
Date: 2027-12-02T10:30:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows

Jasdeep — following up with concrete numbers from infra:

- Warm standby + sticky KV: typical DNS failover + routing = 30–90s. For endpoints that are purely stateless we see median RTO ~45s in our last tabletop tests.
- Full throughput depends on model size and tokenizer warmup: for our recommended medium-sized LLMs (7B–13B quantized) full throughput for concurrent sessions typically returns within 8–12 minutes, 95th percentile up to 15 minutes.
- RPO: audit logs that are persisted to our managed logging tier have near-real-time replication within the same region; cross-region synchronous replication is not currently GA. With the add-on (design/engineering work) we can achieve practical RPO <=1s. Without it, design assumption is potential loss of up to 5 minutes of volatile write buffers.

If Nimbus requires RPO=0 and the synchronous replication add-on we will: 1) scope engineering work, 2) estimate cost and timeline (rough ballpark: $65k engineering + infra delta, 6–8 weeks), and 3) add explicit credit terms in the SOW for staged targets.

I'll produce a short amendment template for procurement to review.

—Ben

Redwood Inference
",
    "From: Jasdeep Singh <jasdeep@nimbushealth.com>

Cc: Nimbus Health Procurement <procurement@nimbushealth.com>, Aria Gomez <aria.gomez@nimbushealth.com>
Date: 2027-12-03T09:00:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Request: multi-region RTO/RPO guarantees for production EHR flows

Thanks — that framing helps a lot. Procurement is OK with the staged failover language provided Redwood includes:

- A defined add-on path priced/committed in the SOW for synchronous cross-region replication to achieve RPO=0 (approximate numbers are acceptable in the amendment)
- Credit table tied to the staged targets you listed (detection, stateless RTO, full capacity recovery)
- A 30-day SLA review window after go-live to validate assumptions and tune replication/caching rules

We can accept a P99 latency up to 700ms during the 15-minute recovery window if credits apply when thresholds are missed. Please send the amendment + redlined SOW and we will route to legal and procurement for signature.

I'll expect the draft amendment by EOD tomorrow.

-Jasdeep
Director of IT Operations
Nimbus Health"

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_0771b119d60346c2903084d9069b6fe3",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-taxonomy-and-ownership-mapping-kickoff.json",
    "title": "Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping — Program kickoff (Reliability Program)",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping \\u2014 Program kickoff (Reliability Program)\",\n  \"space\": \"eng-sre\",\n  \"author\": \"Rafael Mendes\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2025-11-26\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-01-08\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Sean Gallagher\",\n    \"Allison Grant\",\n    \"Ethan Park\",\n    \"Vanessa Ortiz\",\n    \"Sofia Ivanova\",\n    \"Dev Patel\",\n    \"Lauren Bishop\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"reliability\",\n    \"incidents\",\n    \"taxonomy\",\n    \"ownership\",\n    \"sla\",\n    \"oncall\",\n    \"observability\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-taxonomy-v1-definitions.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-ownership-mapping-and-remediation-sla-matrix.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process/incident-classification-policy.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/incident-taxonomy-dashboards-spec.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-0142-incident-taxonomy-as-required-incident-field.json\",\n    \"sources/confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/tying-incident-types-to-slos-and-error-budgets.json\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"body\": \"## Summary\\nThis page kicks off the Reliability Program initiative \\u201cIncident taxonomy + ownership mapping\\u201d. The goal is to reduce incident frequency and improve MTTR by standardizing (1) incident classification, (2) owner accountability, and (3) remediation expectations (SLA timers) across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private tiers.\\n\\nWe are targeting a taxonomy that is:\\n- Easy to apply live during an incident (decision-tree friendly)\\n- Low-cardinality and stable (safe for metric labels and dashboards)\\n- Aligned with real operational control boundaries (single primary owner per type)\\n- Useful for reporting, prioritization, and error budget breakdowns\\n\\n## Why we\\u2019re doing this\\nCurrent incident labeling is inconsistent (freeform tags, service-only naming, inconsistent ownership), which causes:\\n- Ambiguity during response (who owns mitigation vs who is consulted)\\n- Postmortems that are hard to roll up into actionable themes\\n- Dashboards that can\\u2019t reliably show incident drivers by type/team\\n- SLA tracking that varies by commander judgment and tier\\n\\nThe outcome of this initiative is a v1 taxonomy and ownership map that becomes required in incident tooling and postmortems.\\n\\n## Objectives (v1)\\n1) **Standardized incident taxonomy**\\n   - Define a bounded set of top-level incident types and subtypes.\\n   - Provide clear definitions, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and examples.\\n   - Provide a quick decision tree that works under time pressure.\\n\\n2) **Ownership mapping and escalation**\\n   - Map each incident type/subtype to **one primary owning team/service**.\\n   - Define secondary/consulted teams and when to escalate.\\n   - Ensure mappings match actual \\u201ccan mitigate now\\u201d boundaries.\\n\\n3) **Remediation SLAs by tier and severity**\\n   - Define time-to-mitigate (TTM) and time-to-fix (TTF) expectations.\\n   - Align with customer commitments for Hosted/Dedicated/Private.\\n   - Implement timers and breach notifications in tooling.\\n\\n4) **Tooling integration and enforcement**\\n   - incident-bot: required incident_type/subtype + owner resolution.\\n   - postmortems: required taxonomy fields and outcome reporting.\\n   - dashboards/alerts: incident volume, MTTA/MTTR, SLA compliance by type/owner.\\n\\n## Non-goals (v1)\\n- Creating a deep root-cause taxonomy (root cause lives in postmortems; taxonomy is for consistent classification and reporting).\\n- Producing a long-term product roadmap unrelated to incident reduction.\\n- Capturing every edge case on day 1. v1 should be stable; we\\u2019ll iterate with v1.1 after adoption.\\n- Replacing security incident management. This work aligns with security classification, but security incidents remain owned and tracked via Security Ops.\\n\\n## Scope\\n### In-scope incident classes\\nThe taxonomy must cover customer-impacting incidents and high-severity internal incidents that threaten reliability. The initial in-scope set:\\n- **Availability / 5xx / overload** (including saturation and service errors)\\n- **Latency regressions** (p95/p99 and tail latency spikes)\\n- **Streaming disconnects / reset spikes**\\n- **Routing/fallback misbehavior** (wrong policy, wrong fallback target, thrash)\\n- **Capacity/fleet shortages** (GPU scarcity, provisioning lag, regional constraints)\\n- **Control plane outages** (config writes/reads, policy evaluation failures)\\n- **Auth/RBAC failures** (token validation, permission enforcement failures)\\n- **Telemetry/metrics blind spots** (monitoring gaps, missing signals, alert failures)\\n- **Private deployment connectivity/config issues** (VPC/on-prem DNS/TLS, network paths, upgrades)\\n\\n### Out of scope\\n- Purely informational events with no reliability risk (e.g., benign deploy notices).\\n- Low-priority bugs that do not threaten SLOs and do not require incident response.\\n\\n## What \\u201cincident type\\u201d means in this program\\nAn **incident type** is a stable category used for:\\n- paging/triage routing (where applicable)\\n- consistent on-call communication (\\u201cwhat kind of failure is this?\\u201d)\\n- dashboards and reporting (low-cardinality)\\n- accountability (single primary owner)\\n\\nAn incident type is **not**:\\n- the full root cause (\\u201ckernel bug in driver X\\u201d) or a postmortem narrative\\n- a freeform service name (\\u201crouter\\u201d, \\u201cgateway\\u201d, \\u201ck8s\\u201d) without classification intent\\n\\n## Deliverables\\n- **Confluence**\\n  - Taxonomy definitions + decision tree\\n  - Ownership mapping + remediation SLA matrix\\n  - Incident classification policy update\\n  - Postmortem template updates\\n  - ADR: taxonomy required in incident tooling\\n- **Engineering work**\\n  - incident-bot updates (required fields, owner resolution, closure gating)\\n  - control plane config for owner mapping (versioned, reviewed, auditable)\\n  - observability changes (metric label allowlist + guardrails)\\n  - dashboards and breach alerting\\n\\n## Stakeholders and working group\\n### Core working group\\n- **SRE (program lead):** Rafael Mendes\\n- **Executive sponsor (SRE):** Sean Gallagher\\n- **SLO/SLA dashboards:** Aisha Bello\\n- **Observability standards:** Allison Grant\\n- **Dashboards/alerting implementation:** Sergio Costa\\n- **Incident data analysis:** Mei Lin\\n- **Control plane owner mapping:** Ethan Park\\n- **Routing ownership + escalation:** Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon\\n- **Fleet/capacity ownership:** Vanessa Ortiz, Harish Reddy\\n- **Private connectivity/networking:** Victor Alvarez\\n- **Runtime taxonomy SME:** Sofia Ivanova, Noah Patel\\n- **Security alignment:** Fiona McCarthy\\n- **Support/CS escalation mapping:** Dev Patel, Owen Phillips\\n- **Tier SLA stakeholders:** Nikhil Sharma (Hosted), Lauren Bishop (Dedicated), Vivek Kulkarni (Private)\\n- **Tooling integration:** Dylan Brooks, Devon Price\\n- **Docs/training:** Elliot Price, Kira Thompson\\n- **Program management:** Talia Benson\\n\\n### Decision ownership\\n- Taxonomy definitions: SRE + Observability + Runtime/Routing/Fleet SMEs\\n- Primary owner mapping: SRE + owning EM/Director of the mapped team\\n- Remediation SLA targets: SRE + Product/Tier stakeholders + Support/CS\\n- Tooling enforcement: SRE + incident-bot/tooling owners\\n\\n## Cadence and timeline\\nWe\\u2019ll run this as a 6\\u201310 week program with explicit checkpoints.\\n\\n### Cadence\\n- **Weekly working sync (45 min):** SRE + leads from Platform/Routing/Fleet/Runtime/Observability\\n- **Office hours (30 min):** open Q&A for on-call engineers\\n- **Two taxonomy workshops (90 min each):** definitions + decision tree convergence\\n- **Review/signoff window:** async review via Confluence comments + email thread\\n\\n### Proposed phases\\n1) **Discovery + data pull** (Week 1\\u20132)\\n   - Analyze last 90 days incidents + support escalations.\\n   - Propose top 10\\u201315 categories, identify ambiguous clusters.\\n\\n2) **Taxonomy workshop(s)** (Week 2\\u20133)\\n   - Finalize top-level types and the decision tree.\\n   - Confirm \\u201cprimary vs contributing\\u201d guidance for multi-cause incidents.\\n\\n3) **Ownership + SLA alignment** (Week 3\\u20135)\\n   - Validate owners with EMs/Directors.\\n   - Align remediation SLAs with Hosted/Dedicated/Private expectations.\\n\\n4) **Tooling integration** (Week 5\\u20138)\\n   - incident-bot required fields and owner resolution.\\n   - control plane config and audit.\\n   - metric label changes and dashboard rollout.\\n   - SLA timers and breach alerting.\\n\\n5) **Rollout + training + enforcement** (Week 8\\u201310)\\n   - On-call playbook updates.\\n   - Announcement + office hours.\\n   - Enforce classification (cannot close without type/owner).\\n\\n## Success metrics\\nWe will track program success using adoption, data quality, and reliability outcomes.\\n\\n### 1) Classification compliance (adoption)\\n- **>= 90%** of incidents created via incident-bot have incident_type and owner set within **15 minutes** of incident declaration by end of Week 2 post-rollout.\\n- **>= 95%** compliance by end of Week 6 post-rollout.\\n- **< 5%** incidents closed with incident_type = \\u201cUnknown/Unclassified\\u201d by end of Week 6 post-rollout.\\n\\n### 2) Reporting coverage (observability)\\n- Incident dashboards show, at minimum:\\n  - incident volume by incident_type and primary owner\\n  - MTTA/MTTR by incident_type\\n  - remediation SLA breach rate by tier/severity\\n- **>= 90%** of incidents are represented in dashboards with stable labels (no exploding cardinality).\\n\\n### 3) Reliability outcomes (program impact)\\nWe expect a lagging improvement once reporting is stable.\\n- Reduce incidents in top 3 recurring categories by **20% QoQ** (baseline established via 90-day backfill).\\n- Improve median MTTR by **15%** for incidents in categories with clear ownership and playbooks.\\n- Reduce \\u201chandoff time\\u201d (time from incident declare to correct owning team engaged) by **25%**.\\n\\n## Guardrails and constraints\\n- **Low-cardinality taxonomy:** prefer ~10\\u201315 top-level types with small subtype sets.\\n- **Single primary owner:** one accountable team per type/subtype; others listed as secondary/consulted.\\n- **Metric label allowlist:** taxonomy values must be enumerated; \\u201cunknown/unclassified\\u201d is an allowed bucket.\\n- **Tier-aware SLAs:** Dedicated/Private commitments may differ; document carve-outs for cloud-provider force majeure and customer-caused incidents.\\n\\n## Working assumptions\\n- The incident commander (IC) sets initial incident_type during declaration and can update it as evidence changes.\\n- Multi-cause incidents require:\\n  - one primary incident_type for reporting and SLA policy\\n  - contributing systems recorded separately in the incident record/postmortem\\n\\n## Risks and mitigations\\n- **Risk: Taxonomy is too complex to use live**\\n  - Mitigation: decision tree first; keep v1 small; add examples for common confusions.\\n\\n- **Risk: Ownership disputes (Routing vs Fleet vs Runtime vs Platform)**\\n  - Mitigation: map by \\u201cwho can mitigate now\\u201d, not who wrote the code; document escalation and contributing factors.\\n\\n- **Risk: Observability label cardinality blow-up**\\n  - Mitigation: strict allowlist; sampling rules; review by Observability prior to enabling labels broadly.\\n\\n- **Risk: SLAs set unrealistic expectations**\\n  - Mitigation: tier stakeholder signoff; explicit carve-outs; pilot timers before hard enforcement.\\n\\n## Initial decisions (kickoff)\\n- v1 taxonomy will be **mandatory** in incident tooling for new incidents after rollout.\\n- Ownership mapping will be stored in a **versioned, reviewed control-plane config** with audit logs.\\n- We will support \\u201cUnknown/Unclassified\\u201d temporarily, but will treat it as an adoption defect and track reasons.\\n\\n## Open questions\\n- How do we handle incidents that start as \\u201ccapacity\\u201d but are later found to be \\u201crouting policy misbehavior\\u201d? (Proposed: update incident_type; keep contributing factors recorded.)\\n- What are the tier-specific SLA carve-outs for region-wide cloud-provider outages? (Needs final alignment with Dedicated/Private stakeholders.)\\n- What is the appropriate place to store subtype-to-runbook mappings: control plane config vs incident-bot code? (Leaning: control plane config for auditability.)\\n\\n## How to contribute\\n- Comment on the taxonomy draft page with:\\n  - confusing categories and specific incidents that don\\u2019t fit\\n  - suggested examples to add to the decision tree\\n  - ownership boundary concerns (\\u201cwho mitigates this at 3am?\\u201d)\\n- Bring disputed mappings to the weekly sync; SRE will drive to an explicit decision with EM/Director signoff.\\n\\n## Contact and escalation\\n- Program lead: Rafael Mendes (SRE)\\n- Executive sponsor: Sean Gallagher (SRE)\\n- For tooling issues (incident-bot): Dylan Brooks / Devon Price\\n- For observability schema concerns: Allison Grant\\n\\n---\\n### Change log\\n- 2026-01-08: Updated success metrics to include handoff-time target; clarified multi-cause guidance; added initial decisions section.\\n- 2025-11-26: Initial kickoff page created.\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_0771b119d60346c2903084d9069b6fe3\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident taxonomy + ownership mapping — Program kickoff (Reliability Program)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-sre/reliability-initiatives/incident-taxonomy-and-ownership-mapping-kickoff.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: eng-sre\n\nconfidentiality : internal body : # # summary this page kicks off the reliability program initiative “ incident taxonomy + ownership mapping ”. the goal is to reduce incident frequency and improve mttr by standardizing ( 1 ) incident classification, ( 2 ) owner accountability, and ( 3 ) remediation expectations ( sla timers ) across hosted, dedicated, and private tiers. we are targeting a taxonomy that is : - easy to apply live during an incident ( decision - tree friendly ) - low - cardinality and stable ( safe for metric labels and dashboards ) - aligned with real operational control boundaries ( single primary owner per type ) - useful for reporting, prioritization, and error budget breakdowns",
